Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved. The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface. Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports. The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees. Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally. “He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.” View image in fullscreen An African forest elephant. Photograph: Danita Delimont/Alamy Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November.

stories.title: UK sent sex offender refugee to Eswatini in undisclosed deal
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Panoramic view of Mbabane, the capital city of Eswatini in southern Africa By Jean Mackenzie ,Â correspondent ,Â Reporting from Nairobi Â and Â Dominic Casciani ,Â home affairs correspondentÂ Published 25 November 2026 The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community. The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini. The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years. The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died. Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.

My children were unrecognisable. Their bodies were very burned and black, ripped to pieces.” Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.” Ghost strikes: the new drone superpowers raining death from above The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Photograph: Chris Scarffe/Courtesy of Madagasikara Voakajy How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country A s Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar , he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold. “I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.” Rakotoarisoa, 52, patrols the area regularly on behalf of a local group of volunteers and Madagasikara Voakajy, an organisation that protects the island’s endemic species and their habitats.

stories.title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 22 November 2026 Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics. At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40. He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections. "Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC. But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle. Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
